::: {.lesson-meta}
Part 0 · Lesson 3 · About 90 minutes, including setup
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: save points and a shared album"}
In a video game you save before the boss fight, so a mistake costs minutes instead of hours. **Git** gives your project save points, called **commits**, and lets you jump back to any of them. It also lets you try something risky in a parallel timeline (a **branch**) without touching the main one.

**GitHub** is a website that hosts copies of those timelines online, like a shared photo album that teammates can view, copy and suggest additions to. A suggestion to add your photos to someone else's album is a **pull request**.
:::

## Why version control

Without it, projects end up as `final.py`, `final-v2.py`, `final-v2-REALLY.py`. With Git:

- every change is recorded, with who made it, when and why
- you can see exactly what changed between any two points
- you can undo mistakes safely
- several people can work on the same project at once and combine their work

Every company and every open-source project you will ever touch uses Git. PyTorch-Ignite, the project Atlas studies, is developed entirely through Git and GitHub.

## The three places your changes live

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  W[Working folder<br/>files you edit] -->|git add| S[Staging area<br/>changes chosen for<br/>the next commit]
  S -->|git commit| H[History<br/>commits saved<br/>in .git]
  H -->|git push| G[GitHub<br/>shared copy]
  G -->|git pull / git clone| W
```

- The **working folder** is the files you see and edit.
- The **staging area** is a list of changes you have chosen to include in the next commit. It lets you commit some changes and not others.
- The **history** is the chain of commits, stored in a hidden `.git` folder inside your project.
- A **remote** is a copy of the repository somewhere else, usually GitHub.

A **repository** (or **repo**) is a project folder that Git is tracking.

## Install and configure

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Windows (Ubuntu in WSL) and Linux

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git
```

`sudo` runs a command as the administrator; it asks for the password you created when setting up Ubuntu.

## macOS

```bash
xcode-select --install
```

This installs Apple's command-line developer tools, which include Git.
:::

Check it worked, then tell Git who you are. These details are stamped on every commit you make, so use the email you will use for GitHub.

```bash
git --version
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

The last line names the first branch of new repositories `main`, which is the modern convention.

## Your first repository

Here is a real session. Follow along in `~/code`.

```text
$ mkdir -p ~/code/hello-git
$ cd ~/code/hello-git
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/ada/code/hello-git/.git/
$ echo "# Hello Git" > README.md
$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	README.md

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
```

`git status` is the command you will run most. Read it every time: it says which branch you are on and what has changed. **Untracked** means Git sees the file but isn't saving its history yet.

```text
$ git add README.md
$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   README.md

$ git commit -m "docs: Added README"
[main (root-commit) 6b43169] docs: Added README
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 README.md
```

`6b43169` is the commit's **id** (the start of a longer unique code called a hash). Yours will differ.

Now change the file and look at the difference before committing:

```text
$ echo "Learning Git, one commit at a time." >> README.md
$ git diff
diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index ab690e8..98cbc4e 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 # Hello Git
+Learning Git, one commit at a time.
$ git commit -am "docs: Described the project"
$ git log --oneline
1ae4d9c docs: Described the project
6b43169 docs: Added README
```

In a diff, lines starting with `+` were added and lines starting with `-` were removed. `commit -a` stages every change to files Git already tracks, then commits. It never includes brand-new files; those still need `git add`.

### Writing good commit messages

A commit message explains *why* a change was made; the diff already shows *what*. This course uses one consistent style, `type: Past-tense sentence`:

| Type | Use for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `feat` | a new feature | `feat: Added search command` |
| `fix` | a bug fix | `fix: Skipped binary files during search` |
| `docs` | documentation | `docs: Explained the --regex flag` |
| `test` | tests only | `test: Covered empty folders` |
| `chore` | maintenance | `chore: Removed unused imports` |

Keep each commit to one logical change. Small commits are easy to understand, review and undo.

### Ignoring files

Some files should never be committed: passwords, generated files, tool caches. List them in a file called `.gitignore`, one pattern per line:

```text
.venv/
__pycache__/
.env
```

**Never commit a password or secret key.** Deleting it in a later commit doesn't remove it from history; anyone with the repository can still find it. If it happens, treat the secret as leaked and replace it.

## Branches

A **branch** is a separate line of commits. You create one to work on something without disturbing `main`, then **merge** it back when it is ready.

```{mermaid}
gitGraph
  commit id: "Added README"
  commit id: "Described project"
  branch add-notes
  checkout add-notes
  commit id: "Added notes"
  checkout main
  merge add-notes
```

```text
$ git switch -c add-notes
Switched to a new branch 'add-notes'
$ echo "notes" > notes.md
$ git add notes.md
$ git commit -m "docs: Added notes"
$ git switch main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ git merge add-notes
Updating 1ae4d9c..28449c1
Fast-forward
 notes.md | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 notes.md
```

`switch -c` creates a branch and moves onto it. **Fast-forward** means `main` had not changed since the branch started, so Git simply moved `main` forward to include the new commit.

If both branches changed the same lines, Git can't decide which version wins and reports a **merge conflict**. It marks the clashing section in the file between `<<<<<<<` and `>>>>>>>` lines; you edit the file to keep what you want, delete the markers, then `git add` and `git commit`. Conflicts are normal, not a disaster.

## GitHub

1. Create a free account at github.com.
2. Connect your computer with an **SSH key**: a pair of files that proves to GitHub who you are, so you don't type a password each time. The **private key** stays on your computer and is never shared. The **public key** is given to GitHub.

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"
```

Press Enter to accept the default location, and choose a passphrase (or press Enter for none). Then print the public key:

```bash
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

Copy the whole line it prints. On GitHub, open **Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key**, paste it and save. Test the connection:

```bash
ssh -T git@github.com
```

The first time, type `yes` to trust GitHub's server. A greeting containing your username, saying you've successfully authenticated, means it worked.

### Publishing a repository

On GitHub, click **New repository**, name it `hello-git`, leave every box unticked (no README, no .gitignore), and create it. GitHub shows the address to use. Then, in your terminal:

```bash
cd ~/code/hello-git
git remote add origin git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/hello-git.git
git push -u origin main
```

- `remote add origin ...` records GitHub's copy under the name `origin` (the conventional name).
- `push` uploads your commits. `-u` remembers the pairing, so next time `git push` is enough.
- `git pull` does the reverse: downloads new commits from GitHub and merges them in.
- `git clone ADDRESS` downloads a whole repository you don't have yet.

## Pull requests

A **pull request** (PR) is a proposal on GitHub: "please merge the commits on my branch into `main`". It shows the diff, lets people comment line by line, runs automated checks, and records the discussion. Every change to serious projects goes through one, including every change to this course.

The everyday loop:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[git switch -c my-change] --> B[edit, commit]
  B --> C[git push -u origin my-change]
  C --> D[Open a PR on GitHub]
  D --> E[Review and checks]
  E --> F[Merge on GitHub]
  F --> G[git switch main<br/>git pull]
```

## Forks and open source

You can't push branches to someone else's repository. Instead you make a **fork**: your own copy of their repository on GitHub. You push to your fork, then open a pull request from your fork to the original, which is called **upstream**.

This is exactly how you will contribute to PyTorch-Ignite. Good open-source manners:

- **Read `CONTRIBUTING.md` first**, and any other rules files. Ignite also has `AGENTS.md`, with rules for AI-assisted work: AI tools may help you understand, but you must understand the change yourself, and AI must not write issues, pull-request descriptions or replies to reviewers. Atlas is designed to follow those rules.
- **Ask before starting.** Comment on the issue to say you'd like to work on it, and wait for a maintainer to agree.
- **Keep pull requests small** and focused on one thing.
- **Be patient and polite.** Maintainers are often volunteers.

## Get the course and Ignite on your computer

```bash
cd ~/code
git clone https://github.com/ashu-tagore/Learning_FastAPI.git course
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/pytorch/ignite.git ignite
```

- `course` holds the lessons and the reference code in `atlas/`. You read it; you don't work in it.
- `ignite` is the codebase Atlas will study. `--depth 1` downloads only the latest commit, which is much smaller; that's all Part 1 needs.

Your own code will live in your own repository, `my-atlas`, which you create in lesson 1.1.

## Common mistakes

- **Committing secrets.** Add `.env` to `.gitignore` before you ever create one.
- **One giant commit at the end of the day.** Commit each small step that works.
- **Working directly on `main`** for anything bigger than a typo. Use a branch.
- **Forgetting to pull** before starting work, then hitting conflicts. Start each session with `git pull`.
- **Force-pushing** (`git push --force`) to a shared branch. It overwrites other people's work. You won't need it in this course.
- **Panicking at a conflict.** Read the markers, choose the right lines, commit. That's all it is.

## Check yourself

**1.** You edited `a.py` and `b.py` but only want `a.py` in the next commit. What do you run?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`git add a.py` then `git commit -m "..."`. Only staged changes go into a commit; `b.py` stays modified in your working folder for a later commit. (`git commit -a` would have included both.)
:::

**2.** What is the difference between a branch and a fork?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A **branch** is a separate line of commits inside one repository. A **fork** is a whole copy of someone else's repository under your GitHub account. You fork when you can't push to the original; then you create branches inside your fork and open pull requests from them.
:::

**3.** You accidentally committed a file containing a password and pushed it. You delete the file and commit again. Is the password safe now?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. The old commit still contains it, and anyone can read history. Change the password (treat it as leaked) and make sure the file is listed in `.gitignore` from now on.
:::

## Exercise: your first pull request

1. Push `hello-git` to GitHub as shown above.
2. Create a branch `add-goals`. Add a file `goals.md` listing three things you want to build in this course. Commit it with a message in the course's style.
3. Push the branch: `git push -u origin add-goals`.
4. On GitHub, open a pull request from `add-goals` into `main`. Read the "Files changed" tab, then merge it.
5. Back in the terminal, switch to `main` and pull. Confirm `goals.md` is there and `git log --oneline` shows your commit.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```bash
cd ~/code/hello-git
git switch -c add-goals
echo "- Build Atlas" > goals.md
echo "- Deploy to AWS" >> goals.md
echo "- Contribute to PyTorch-Ignite" >> goals.md
git add goals.md
git commit -m "docs: Added my course goals"
git push -u origin add-goals
# open and merge the pull request on github.com
git switch main
git pull
ls
git log --oneline
```

If `git pull` says "There is no tracking information", run `git push -u origin main` once to pair `main` with GitHub, then pull again.
:::

## Stretch: read a real project's history and rules

In your Ignite clone:

1. Open `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `AGENTS.md` in your editor. Find: the command to run the code-style checks, and two things AI agents must not do.
2. On GitHub, open Ignite's issues and filter by the label `good first issue`. Pick one and read the whole discussion.
3. Run `git log --oneline -5` in the clone. Why do you see only one commit?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
1. `pre-commit run --all-files` (it runs `ruff` for linting and formatting). Agents must not open issues or pull requests, and must not write pull-request descriptions, commit messages or replies to reviewers on the user's behalf. (Rules change; always read the current files.)
2. Notice how the discussion goes: someone describes a problem, often with a small code example that shows it (a reproduction); a maintainer confirms; a contributor asks to work on it. Atlas Agents will prepare exactly that kind of understanding for you.
3. You cloned with `--depth 1`, which downloads only the latest commit. `git fetch --unshallow` would download the full history when you need it.
:::

## What changed in the project

You can now save, branch, publish and propose changes. You have three folders in `~/code`: `hello-git` (practice), `course` (lessons and reference code) and `ignite` (the codebase Atlas will search). Part 1 starts your own project, `my-atlas`.
